title: Cap. II Arg. 3: 1 Cor. 2:9 — prepared for those who love him (king/crown analogy)
latin: Tertio, affertur illud ex 1. Cor. ii. 9. Oculus non vidit, &c. quae praeparavit Deus iis qui diligunt illum. Verba illa, iis qui diligunt illum, secundum communem loquendi modum ipsam causam praeparationis indicant. Nam si quis diceret Regem praeparasse aut destinasse coronam adscendentibus muros oppugnatae alicujus civitatis, hoc dicto significaret ex praevisione adscensionis hanc coronam esse huic vel illi destinatam, & non aliter.
pass_a: Thirdly, that place is brought from 1 Cor. ii. 9. Eye hath not seen, &c. the things which God hath prepared for them that love him. Those words, for them that love him, according to the common manner of speaking, indicate the very cause of the preparation. For if one should say that a King had prepared or destined a crown for those ascending the walls of some city under assault, by that saying he would signify that from foresight of the ascent this crown was destined to this or that man, and not otherwise.
pass_b: Third: they bring 1 Cor. 2:9 — "Eye has not seen… the things God prepared for those who love him." On ordinary speech, "for those who love him" looks like the cause of the preparation. Say a king prepared a crown for whoever scales a besieged city's walls: that would mean the crown was destined to this or that man from foresight of the climb — and no other way.

lemmas.gloss: things prepared for those who love him
adversaries take love as cause of preparation
king/crown analogy from foresight of ascent

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 3: love shows who receive glory — not foresight-cause of the decree
latin: Verba illa, iis qui diligunt eum, ostendunt nobis quales tandem illi omnes sint, quibus ab aeterno gloriam praeparavit: sed non indicant hanc dilectionem praevisam fuisse causam aut rationem cur gloria fuit illis destinata. Idem amor Dei qui eos destinavit gratuito ad gloriam, destinavit etiam eos ad hanc dilectionem Dei, qua impellente viam ineunt quae recte ducit ad gloriam. Est itaque nostra Dei dilectio effectum amoris Divini quo nos elegit & praedestinavit ad salutem, atque idcirco inepte supponitur causa nostrae electionis. Huc spectant illa Apostoli verba, Nos diligimus Deum quia ipse prior dilexit nos. 1 Joan. iv. 19.
pass_a: Those words, for them that love him, show us of what sort finally all those are for whom from eternity he prepared glory: but they do not indicate that this love foreseen was the cause or reason why glory was destined to them. The same love of God which destined them freely unto glory also destined them unto this love of God, by which, being driven, they enter the way that rightly leads unto glory. Our love of God therefore is an effect of the Divine love by which he elected and predestinated us unto salvation, and therefore it is foolishly supposed as the cause of our election. Hither look those words of the Apostle, We love God because he first loved us. 1 John iv. 19.
pass_b: Reply: "for those who love him" tells what sort of people finally receive the glory he prepared from eternity — it does not make foresight of that love the cause why glory was destined to them. The same love that freely destined them to glory also destined them to love God, and by that love they take the road that leads to glory. So our love of God is an effect of the divine love that elected and predestined us to salvation — foolishly taken as election's cause. So the Apostle: "We love God because he first loved us" (1 John 4:19).

lemmas.gloss: our love of God is effect, not cause, of election
we love because he first loved
same decree destines to glory and to loving God

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 3: Augustine In Joh. 86 — praescientia pleaded against grace
latin: Optime Augustinus, in Johan. tract. 86. Praescientiam Dei defendunt contra gratiam Dei, qui dicunt nos electos ante mundi constitutionem quia praescivit nos Deus futuros bonos. Non enim electi sunt quia boni fuerunt, qui boni non essent nisi electi essent. Quidni igitur & nos dicamus, eos praescientiam Dei defendere contra gratiam Dei, qui dicunt nos electos, quia Deus praescivit nos ut illum diligentes? cum utique Dei amantes nunquam essemus nisi electi fuissemus.
pass_a: Most excellently Augustine, on John, tractate 86: They defend the foreknowledge of God against the grace of God, who say we were elected before the foundation of the world because God foresaw that we would be good. For they were not elected because they were good, who would not have been good unless they had been elected. Why then should not we also say that they defend the foreknowledge of God against the grace of God, who say we were elected because God foresaw us as loving him? since assuredly we should never be lovers of God unless we had been elected.
pass_b: Augustine (In John, tract. 86) puts it best: they defend God's foreknowledge against his grace when they say we were elect before the world's foundation because God foresaw we would be good. They were not elect because they were good — they would not have been good unless elect. So we may say the same of those who claim we were elect because God foresaw us as loving him: we would never love God unless we had been elect.

lemmas.gloss: not elect because good; good because elect
foresight of loving God cannot ground election

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 3: earthly king analogy fails — strength from crown's destination
latin: Postremo, quod attinet ad similitudinem allatam de Rege terreno coronam destinante adscendentibus muros civitatis; ingentem habet dissimilitudinem in illa ipsa re, unde tota vis argumenti dependet. Nam si nemo possit suis viribus adscendere, & Rex ille possit vires hasce quibus visum fuerit inspirare, non jam illis quibus hasce vires tribueret, destinata fuisset corona ex praevisione adscensionis; sed praevisa adscensio & vires inspiratae, ex destinatione coronae. At sic res habet planissime inter Deum & homines.
pass_a: Lastly, as to the likeness brought of an earthly King destining a crown to those ascending the walls of a city: it has an immense unlikeness in that very point on which the whole force of the argument depends. For if no one could ascend by his own powers, and that King could inspire these powers into whomsoever he pleased, the crown would no longer have been destined to those to whom he would grant these powers from foresight of the ascent; but the foresight of the ascent and the inspired powers would be from the destination of the crown. And thus the matter stands most plainly between God and men.
pass_b: Last: the earthly-king crown analogy fails at the very hinge of the argument. If no one could climb by his own strength, and the king could breathe that strength into whomever he chose, the crown would not be destined from foresight of the climb — the climb foreseen, and the strength given, would flow from the crown's destination. That is exactly how it stands between God and men.

lemmas.gloss: king analogy breaks when climb requires infused strength
inspired powers from destination of the crown

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 3 close: love infused from election — Augustine De grat. Christi 26
latin: Nemo Deum diligeret, nisi Deus charitatem illi infunderet; nemini charitatem salutiferam infunderet, nisi eum prius ad salutem destinasset. Non ergo ex praevisione dilectionis nostrae destinat nobis vitam aeternam, sed ex proposito electionis ad vitam aeternam infundit nobis hanc dilectionem. Concludamus hoc responsum nostrum verbis Augustini, qui mallei instar ubique contundit Pelagianos. Sic ergo ille, Ut acciperemus dilectionem qua diligeremus, dilecti sumus, cum eam nondum haberemus. De grat. Christi contr. Pelag. cap. 26.
pass_a: No one would love God unless God infused charity into him; he would infuse saving charity into no one unless he had first destined him unto salvation. Therefore he does not destine eternal life to us from foresight of our love, but from the purpose of election unto eternal life he infuses this love into us. Let us conclude this our answer with the words of Augustine, who like a hammer everywhere bruises the Pelagians. Thus therefore he: That we might receive the love with which we should love, we were loved, when we did not yet have it. On the Grace of Christ against Pelagius, chapter 26.
pass_b: No one would love God unless God poured charity into him; God would pour saving charity into no one unless he had first destined him to salvation. So he does not destine eternal life from foresight of our love — from the purpose of election to eternal life he infuses that love. Close with Augustine, who hammers the Pelagians everywhere: "That we might receive the love with which we should love, we were loved when we did not yet have it" (On the Grace of Christ against Pelagius, ch. 26).

lemmas.gloss: saving charity infused only after destination to salvation
loved before we had love to love with
